We find several limitations in our methods. For example, LMs:
1) struggle to make examples for concepts they don’t understand well.
2) sometimes include social biases.
3) are sensitive to the phrasing of the generation instructions.
4) sometimes produce overly similar examples.

author: AnthropicAI
text: In our paper we used an ad hoc constitution drafted purely for research purposes. Ultimately, we think constitutions shouldn’t be just defined by researchers in isolation, but by groups of experts from different disciplines working together.

author: AnthropicAI
text: While the name “Constitutional AI” may sound ambitious, we chose it to emphasize that powerful, general-purpose AI systems will always be operating according to *some* principles, even if they are left implicit, or encoded in privately held data.

author: AnthropicAI
text: We then distill these examples of “AI Feedback” into a single preference model, and use RL to train a final assistant whose behavior is governed by the constitution.

author: AnthropicAI
text: Then in a second “RLAIF” phase,  the AI explores possible responses to thousands of prompts, and uses chain-of-thought reasoning to identify the behavior that is most consistent with its constitution. https://t.co/L0KJwcw2J9

author: AnthropicAI
text: The AI uses these principles for self-improvement. In a first, supervised learning phase, the AI writes responses to a wide variety of prompts, revises these initial responses in accordance with the constitution, and then imitates its revisions via supervised learning. https://t.co/7hGIImJ9Xx

author: AnthropicAI
text: How does it work?  With CAI, we trained a harmless assistant using a list of ~10 natural language instructions or principles which, taken together, form the “Constitution” (our initial list was purely for research purposes).

text: CAI lets us fix mistakes with AI behavior or specifically target new goals in just a few days, simply by changing the instructions we provide - it’s much more efficient than finetuning on large RLHF datasets. https://t.co/ptm1wwt3yv

author: AnthropicAI
text: The ideas in this paper build on lots of previous work, including papers hypothesizing the existence of superposition. It's also connected to ideas in compressed sensing, distributed representations, disentanglement, and other work.

author: AnthropicAI
text: If superposition is widespread, understanding it will be essential for interpretability (especially models like transformers where polysemanticity is dominant). This is a small first step to understanding it.

author: AnthropicAI
text: We also find that neural nets can do simple computation on features while they're in superposition. This suggests a wild possibility: neural networks may, in some sense, be simulating larger sparse models.

author: AnthropicAI
text: Amazingly, features in superposition are organized into subspaces with geometry corresponding to regular polytopes (pentagons, tetrahedra) and other solutions to the Thomson problem. This creates discretized “energy levels” in the amount of dimensionality allocated to features. https://t.co/H4HnaS0ea3

author: AnthropicAI
text: It turns out that whether a feature is stored in a dedicated dimension, not learned at all, or represented in superposition is governed by a discontinuous phase change between three regimes! https://t.co/Y60tbvp3Wt

author: AnthropicAI
text: Superposition doesn't occur in linear models. It only occurs if one introduces a non-linearity that can filter out noise from superposition "interference". It also requires sparsity: as features become sparser, there is more superposition. https://t.co/eg2oEM59I6

author: AnthropicAI
text:
For example, if a word embedding has 512 dimensions, one might think it has 512 features (eg. verb-noun, male-female, singular-plural, …). Superposition suggests there may be many more – they're just not exactly orthogonal.

(This is very similar to ideas in compressed sensing!)

author: AnthropicAI
text:
If a neural network has 𝑛 feature dimensions, you might intuitively expect that it will store 𝑛 different features. But it turns out that neural networks can store more than 𝑛 features in "superposition" if the features are sparse!
https://t.co/B7pYjoJPHF https://t.co/Wo6oRrDsfG

author: AnthropicAI
text: Neural networks often pack many unrelated concepts into a single neuron – a puzzling phenomenon known as 'polysemanticity' which makes interpretability much more challenging. In our latest work, we build toy models where the origins of polysemanticity can be fully understood.

author: AnthropicAI
text: We find that the data we generate from red teaming allows us to build safer (but far from perfect) systems. Attacks against the 52B RLHF model still succeed 15% of the time, compared to 43% of the time for the 52B plain LM. (This illustrates some of the problems of RLHF models).

author: AnthropicAI
text: We red team four types of language models: a plain LM; a LM prompted to be helpful, harmless, and honest (HHH); a LM with rejection sampling (RS) against a helpful and harmless preference model; and a model trained to be helpful and harmless with RL from human feedback (RLHF).

author: AnthropicAI
text:
Co-occurrence during the phase change is one of 6 arguments we present, forming a circumstantial case that induction heads might drive the majority of in-context learning in state-of-the-art transformers.

These findings aren’t definitive, and alternative hypotheses are possible.

author: AnthropicAI
text:
Our last paper introduced “induction heads”.

These heads implement a simple algorithm that completes token sequences like [A][B] … [A] → [B]

(They aren’t memorized n-grams, because they work on *completely random* tokens)

The “phase change” is precisely when they develop! https://t.co/0kkDQxIukx

author: AnthropicAI
text:
We study 34 transformers over the course of training.

All models (except the 1-layer) abruptly get better at “in-context learning” after a few billion tokens.

Studying what happens during this “phase change” gives us evidence about the mechanisms driving in-context learning. https://t.co/KRw9MXzcqt

author: AnthropicAI
text:
In our second interpretability paper, we revisit “induction heads”.

In 2+ layer transformers these pattern-completion heads form exactly when in-context learning abruptly improves.

Are they responsible for most in-context learning in large transformers?

https://t.co/28WWkMrjQm
